analysis.one_liner: Requires billion-dollar corporations to get federal charters, seat workers on boards, and get approval for political spending.
analysis.headline: The Accountable Capitalism Act was introduced in the House in December 2018 with 4 cosponsors, referred to five committees, and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any company with more than $1 billion in annual revenue to obtain a federal corporate charter from a new Office of United States Corporations. Charters would carry duties: at least 40% of board seats elected by employees, a legal duty to consider workers, customers, and communities alongside shareholders, restrictions on when executives can sell company stock, shareholder approval for political spending, and possible revocation of the charter for repeated serious misconduct. It was referred to five House committees and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of the roughly 1,800–2,000 US companies with over $1 billion in revenue would gain guaranteed representation on corporate boards. Workers, customers, and communities would gain standing through directors required to weigh their interests alongside shareholder returns. Shareholders would gain a veto over the company's political spending, and the public would gain restrictions on executive stock cash-outs and a mechanism to strip the charter of companies engaged in repeated serious misconduct.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and shareholders of billion-dollar corporations

how_it_helps.text: Every large entity (over $1 billion in gross receipts, with affiliated companies aggregated) must obtain a federal charter, and the charter must state a purpose of creating a 'general public benefit' beyond shareholder profit.
Directors and officers must balance shareholder interests with those of employees, suppliers, customers, communities, and the environment, and must consider effects on those groups when acting.

At least two-fifths of the directors of each chartered corporation must be elected by its employees, under rules set by the SEC in consultation with the National Labor Relations Board, with daily fines of $50,000–$100,000 for noncompliance.

Executives and directors cannot sell company stock for 5 years after acquiring it, or for 3 years after the company buys back its own shares, with civil penalties of 1 to 3 times the value of the stock sold.

Corporations cannot spend money on political campaigns (independent expenditures, electioneering communications, or pass-through payments) without approval from 75% of shareholders and 75% of directors, with shareholder lawsuits and charter revocation as enforcement.

A state attorney general may petition to revoke a corporation's charter for 'repeated, egregious, and illegal misconduct' causing significant harm that the company has not remedied, such as by firing the executives responsible.

analysis.who_pays: Executives and directors of large corporations, who would face new limits on selling stock and would share board control with employees; and large corporations generally, which would bear charter compliance costs, pay fines for noncompliance, and lose unilateral control over political spending. Some compliance costs could be passed to consumers, and companies could relocate some activity below the $1 billion threshold.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to every entity over $1 billion in gross receipts, including LLCs and aggregated affiliated companies, so it sweeps in thousands of mid-size firms and imposes real chartering, reporting, and compliance costs that could be passed on to consumers and could push some companies to restructure to stay under the threshold.

Directors are explicitly not required to prioritize any one interest and are shielded from personal liability for failing to create the public benefit, and only shareholders (2% of shares) can sue to enforce the duties — so the 'public benefit' mandate relies heavily on employee-elected directors having real influence rather than on outside enforcement.

The federal charter requirement is a major expansion of federal power over corporate governance, which has historically been state law; critics of the Senate companion bill argued it raised serious constitutional questions about Congress's authority over purely intrastate business and that revoking charters could strip companies of legal standing needed to operate and pay workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give employees board representation and curb executive stock cash-outs and unilateral corporate political spending, changes aimed at the two practices most cited for short-term pressure on workers and wages. The trade-offs are real: the $1 billion revenue threshold is a blunt instrument that catches far more than the giant firms targeted, the public-benefit mandate is weakly enforceable from outside the company, and the federal chartering structure raises constitutional questions that would likely have ended up in court. The bill never advanced far enough for any of these issues to be tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 13, 2018 and referred to five House committees, and none of them took it up before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so it expired without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ben Ray Luján introduced the Accountable Capitalism Act in the House on December 13, 2018, with four Democratic cosponsors (Reps. Boyle, Lynch, Pocan, and Schakowsky).

The bill was referred to five committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Financial Services, House Administration, and Education and the Workforce — a multi-referral that required several committees to act before the bill could advance.
The action history shows no further activity after the initial referral: no hearings, no markups, no committee votes, and no floor action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The bill would have created an Office of United States Corporations in the Commerce Department to grant and revoke charters for companies with over $1 billion in gross receipts.
Under the bill, failure to obtain a required charter would mean the entity is no longer treated as a corporation for purposes of federal law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and directors of billion-dollar corporations are better off because the bill died: they keep sole control of their boards, retain the ability to sell stock on their current timeline, and keep unilateral control over corporate political spending. The Republican House majority that never scheduled the bill also kept it off the record entirely.

for.name: Rep. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Accountable Capitalism Act in the House on December 13, 2018.

for.name: Reps. Brendan Boyle, Stephen Lynch, Mark Pocan, and Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other members joined.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.role: Author of the Senate companion bill (S. 3348, 115th Congress)
for.what_they_did: Proposed the Accountable Capitalism Act in the Senate in August 2018; the House bill was its companion.

against.name: Republican House majority
against.role: 115th Congress House leadership and the chairs of the five referred committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or floor vote in any of the five committees to which it was referred, and never brought it to the floor before the Congress ended.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and large-business trade groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the Accountable Capitalism Act, calling the federal chartering and employee-board provisions harmful to competitiveness.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat and no Republican supported the bill; with Republicans controlling the House, committees and leadership never acted on it.

industries.industry: Large corporations (over $1 billion in gross receipts)
industries.note: The bill would require them to obtain federal charters, cede 40% of board seats to employees, restrict executive stock sales, and require 75% shareholder and director approval for political spending — all of which dilute management's control and add compliance costs. Ordinary people would gain the board representation and checks the bill creates.

industries.industry: Corporate executives and directors of large companies
industries.note: Executives would face a 5-year lockup on selling company stock and a 3-year ban after buybacks, plus civil penalties up to triple the value of sales in violation — directly limiting a major source of executive wealth extraction.

industries.industry: Corporate political spending channels (trade associations and outside groups funded by corporate dues)
industries.note: The bill requires 75% shareholder and director approval for political expenditures over $10,000 per candidate, including dues and transfers that could be used for electioneering — cutting off the routine routing of corporate money to outside political groups.
